segments.text: When you ask an AI a question, it first works out what your words mean together.
But then it faces a new problem.
How exactly does it begin an answer?
To see how this works, we will treat individual words as single tokens
to make our example easy to follow.
This diagram shows what happens right before the answer begins.
When you ask, what should I name my new dog?
The question goes through four distinct processing steps.
First, the AI breaks your question into token pieces.
Next, it marks the precise position where each of those pieces belongs.
For step 3, the system turns each token into starting vectors,
numbers that carry their initial meaning.
Finally, in step 4, those numbers pass through the model's layers,
where attention and transformation work together to update them.
Before a single letter of the response is generated,
your entire question is mapped out as a complex mathematical context.
As those tokens pass through the layers,
every token's vector is updated using information from the tokens that came before it.
This comparison diagram shows exactly how preceding words change token's math.
Let's look at the question mark at the very end of our prompt.
In the first box, for the question, what should I name my new dog?
The question mark's updated vector reflects naming a dog.
But in the second box, what should I cook for dinner?
That exact same symbol now has a vector reflecting a choice about a meal.
Because it sits at the very end of the prompt,
that final question mark acts as a container.
Its updated vector holds the accumulated, unique context of your entire specific question.
The AI uses that final token's updated vector to predict the very first token of its answer.
This interface shows the AI's first prediction.
The model hasn't written any part of the answer yet,
but it generates a menu of possible starts.
Based on the math, u has an 18% chance of being the next word,
a sits at 14%, great is at 9%,
and all other possible tokens make up the remaining 59%.
From these calculations, the AI makes its selection and chooses u to begin its reply.
The AI does not pull a pre-written answer from a database.
It calculates the odds for every possible word and makes a selection from those probabilities.
Once u is selected, it is immediately added to the context.
It becomes the new final token,
and its updated vector now reflects both your original question and the single word reply so far.
The cycle repeats.
The AI calculates and adds could, then name, and then him.
Every newly added token is immediately folded into the growing context.
This screen shows the next prediction step.
The prompt is still, what should I name my new dog?
And the answer so far is, you could name him.
The accumulated context now strongly points to a dog's name.
The probabilities reflect this shift.
Spot jumps to a 22% likelihood.
Max is at 17%, Buddy at 14%, with all other tokens accounting for 47%.
The AI selects spot based on these odds, finalizing the name.
Because the entire system runs on probabilities,
running the exact same prompt again could yield a completely different selection, like Max.
After outputting spot, the AI repeats the process one more time to predict and add a period.
But a punctuation mark doesn't halt the system.
The AI ultimately generates a special hidden end-of-answer token.
That specific token acts as a hard stop, signaling that the reply is 100% complete.
This graphic summarizes the core mechanism.
Every answer is built exactly like this, one token at a time.
And this entire start-to-finish sequence is called inference.
